newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec premier jumps into Canada election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Quebec premier jumps into Canada election campaign.

text.p: Just two weeks before Canada goes to the polls in a June 2 federal election, Quebec premier Lucien Bouchard has jumped in to salvage a disastrous campaign by Bloc Quebecois leader Gilles Duceppe.

In a desperate attempt to shore up his ailing campaign, Duceppe announced on Monday night that even former Quebec premier Jacques Parizeau, who resigned in 1995, will be enlisted to campaign for the Bloc, which supports the separation of French-speaking Quebec from the rest of Canada.

Parizeau is already embroiled in a controversy sparked by a new book in which he says he would have made an unilateral declaration of independence for Quebec if the province had won a 1995 sovereignty referendum.
The Bloc Quebecois, the largest opposition party in Canada's parliament until this election, is an oddity: a separatist party acting within the federal political system.

In an impassioned speech in the separatist stronghold of the Saguenay on Monday, Bouchard launched an offensive against Jean Charest, the leader of Canada's Conservative Party and the most popular federal politician in Quebec.
Recent polls have shown there is a three-way race in Quebec between the Bloc Quebecois, the Conservatives and the ruling Liberal party of Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien.
Support for the Bloc Quebecois has been slipping across the province following numerous gaffes by Duceppe, prompting Bouchard to jump into the campaign.
"The choice is between Jean Chretien's blank cheque and Jean Charest's black hole," declared Bouchard.
Bouchard attacked Charest for diluting the failed 1990 Meech Lake constitutional accord, which would have recognised Quebec as a distinct society within Canada.
Bouchard, who was then a minister in Brian Mulroney's Conservative government, quit the cabinet in 1990 to create the Bloc Quebecois.

"If anyone knows that you can't rely on Ottawa to defend Quebec's interests, it's me," said an emotional Bouchard in his home district of Jonquiere. "I know. I have paid the price for that. The only solution is sovereignty."
Under the new strategy, Bouchard and his separatists aim to depict both Chretien and Charest as bent on crushing the separatist movement.
In the 1993 election, Charest was the only Conservative member of parliament elected in Quebec, and one of only two voted in nationwide.

Two polls published on Saturday showed the Conservatives gaining strongly in Quebec, largely at the expense of the Bloc Quebecois. The separatist party's campaign has been falling apart steadily over the past two weeks, mainly because of negative public perceptions of Duceppe.
